context: Three production-relevant requirement families: demand determinants, PED, YED. Complete the 18 previously unauthored provisional research skills without claiming independent educational acceptance.

skill_specimens.original_case: A competing brand's refill capsules rise from £6 to £7 while Revision's fictional capsules remain £5.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: A rise in the price of a substitute can shift demand for the unchanged-price product to the right because some consumers switch brands.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Explain the likely effect on demand for the £5 capsules.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: A rise in the price of a substitute can shift demand for the unchanged-price product to the right because some consumers switch brands.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: Do not call this a movement along the £5 product's demand curve. Substitutability and customer awareness matter.

skill_specimens.original_case: A fictional reusable-bottle system needs a compatible filter, but the bottle price rises while filter prices are unchanged.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: If fewer bottles are bought at the higher bottle price, demand for their complementary filters may fall at each filter price.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Explain the likely effect on demand for the compatible filters.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: If fewer bottles are bought at the higher bottle price, demand for their complementary filters may fall at each filter price.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: Whether the change is significant depends on existing bottle owners and the ability to use alternative filters.

skill_specimens.original_case: Household incomes rise in a fictional town. Sales of premium lunches increase, while some shoppers replace low-cost instant meals.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: For households treating premium lunches as normal goods, higher incomes can shift their demand right. Demand for instant meals could fall if consumers regard them as inferior alternatives.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Explain two possible income effects on demand.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: For households treating premium lunches as normal goods, higher incomes can shift their demand right. Demand for instant meals could fall if consumers regard them as inferior alternatives.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: Normal or inferior is a consumer-behaviour classification, not a fixed property of every food item.

skill_specimens.original_case: An original school survey suggests more students prefer reusable lunch boxes to disposable packaging, with prices unchanged.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: An increase in preference for reusable boxes can shift their demand curve right at any given own price.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Predict a plausible demand change for reusable boxes.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: An increase in preference for reusable boxes can shift their demand curve right at any given own price.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: Survey intentions are not certain purchases; distinguish demand shifts from movements caused by the product's price.

skill_specimens.original_case: A fictional refill-pack brand launches a campaign explaining its product while holding price steady.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: An effective campaign can improve awareness or preferences and increase the quantity demanded at every given price, shifting the demand curve right.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Explain how advertising could affect market demand.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: An effective campaign can improve awareness or preferences and increase the quantity demanded at every given price, shifting the demand curve right.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: The result is conditional on campaign credibility, reach and competitors' reactions; advertising alone guarantees nothing.

skill_specimens.original_case: A fictional campus adds 1,000 resident students. The campus canteen sells fixed-price lunch boxes.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: More potential buyers can shift demand for lunch boxes to the right at unchanged prices if the new students buy them.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Explain the possible effect on market demand for lunch boxes.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: More potential buyers can shift demand for lunch boxes to the right at unchanged prices if the new students buy them.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: Changing demographics affects market size and composition, not necessarily each person's demand; onsite alternatives matter.

skill_specimens.original_case: A local rail shutdown reduces city-centre footfall for two weeks, while takeaway coffee prices remain fixed.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: Fewer commuters could reduce demand for city-centre takeaway coffee at each price, shifting demand left.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Explain a plausible demand effect and limitation.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: Fewer commuters could reduce demand for city-centre takeaway coffee at each price, shifting demand left.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: Delivery customers and local residents may offset some of the decline; the shock may be temporary.

skill_specimens.original_case: An original umbrella retailer sees wet winter weather after a dry summer. Its prices do not change.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: Seasonal conditions can increase willingness to buy umbrellas at a given price, moving the whole demand curve right.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Explain the likely seasonal demand effect at unchanged selling prices.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: Seasonal conditions can increase willingness to buy umbrellas at a given price, moving the whole demand curve right.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: Actual impact depends on weather severity and inventories; it is not a movement along the demand curve.

skill_specimens.original_case: A fictional stationery shop raises its price from £5 to £5.50. Units demanded fall from 200 to 170 per week.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: Quantity changes by -15% and price rises by 10%, so PED = -15% / 10% = -1.5; the negative sign indicates the usual inverse relationship.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Calculate price elasticity of demand using percentage changes from initial values.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: Quantity changes by -15% and price rises by 10%, so PED = -15% / 10% = -1.5; the negative sign indicates the usual inverse relationship.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: The initial-value method is specified for this research item; midpoint/arc methods give different figures.

skill_specimens.original_case: Two fictional services report estimated price elasticities of demand of -0.4 and -1.8.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: -0.4 is relatively inelastic: a 1% rise in price is associated with roughly 0.4% lower quantity demanded, other factors unchanged. -1.8 is elastic: around 1.8% less.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Interpret the two values and distinguish relative responsiveness.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: -0.4 is relatively inelastic: a 1% rise in price is associated with roughly 0.4% lower quantity demanded, other factors unchanged. -1.8 is elastic: around 1.8% less.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: These are local estimates rather than guaranteed responses to large price changes.

skill_specimens.original_case: A fictional café sells a drink with many close substitutes; a unique specialist service has few alternatives.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: More close substitutes tend to make consumers more price responsive. A specialist service without alternatives may face relatively inelastic demand; consumers also adjust more over time.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Compare two influences on PED and identify a limitation of each comparison.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: More close substitutes tend to make consumers more price responsive. A specialist service without alternatives may face relatively inelastic demand; consumers also adjust more over time.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: Habit, necessity and relative expenditure may override the simple substitute comparison.

skill_specimens.original_case: A fictional seller lowers price from £10 to £9; weekly quantity demanded increases from 100 to 125 units.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: Revenue increases from £1,000 to £1,125, so a price reduction increases revenue by £125; initial-base PED is +25% / -10% = -2.5, indicating elastic demand.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Calculate the change in revenue and discuss a pricing implication.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: Revenue increases from £1,000 to £1,125, so a price reduction increases revenue by £125; initial-base PED is +25% / -10% = -2.5, indicating elastic demand.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: Higher revenue need not mean higher profit: production costs and competitor responses also matter.

skill_specimens.original_case: A fictional store raises its price from £4 to £5 and sales fall from 100 to 85 units.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: Initial revenue is £4 × 100 = £400; final revenue is £5 × 85 = £425; revenue rises by £25 even though quantity falls.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Calculate revenue before and after the price change.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: Initial revenue is £4 × 100 = £400; final revenue is £5 × 85 = £425; revenue rises by £25 even though quantity falls.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: A revenue calculation is not itself evidence of profit or a guaranteed future PED.

skill_specimens.original_case: An original retailer increases unit price from £4 to £5 and sells 85 rather than 100 items. Revenue therefore rises from £400 to £425.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: The increase improves sales revenue by £25 in this example, consistent with a relatively inelastic initial-price response. Whether to maintain it depends on margins, retention and longer-run consumer reactions.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Assess whether the firm should permanently keep the higher price.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: The increase improves sales revenue by £25 in this example, consistent with a relatively inelastic initial-price response. Whether to maintain it depends on margins, retention and longer-run consumer reactions.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: Do not mistake short-run revenue for profit, or infer that the same elasticity will persist.

skill_specimens.original_case: In a fictional town, average monthly income rises from £2,500 to £2,750 and premium lunch sales rise from 80 to 96 per week.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: Demand increases by 20% and income increases by 10%; YED = 20% / 10% = +2.0, indicating an income-responsive normal good in this case.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Calculate income elasticity of demand using initial values.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: Demand increases by 20% and income increases by 10%; YED = 20% / 10% = +2.0, indicating an income-responsive normal good in this case.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: The classification follows these hypothetical observations; it does not establish a stable elasticity at all incomes.

skill_specimens.original_case: Fictional estimates suggest a budget meal has YED -0.6 and a premium excursion has YED +1.4.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: At those observations the budget meal behaves as an inferior good: higher income is associated with lower demand. The excursion behaves as an income-elastic normal good.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Explain the business meaning of both estimates.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: At those observations the budget meal behaves as an inferior good: higher income is associated with lower demand. The excursion behaves as an income-elastic normal good.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: The same product could behave differently across income groups and economic conditions.

skill_specimens.original_case: A fictional retailer sells essential toiletries and optional luxury gift boxes.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: Consumers typically continue buying necessities when income changes, which may yield low positive YED; discretionary luxuries may have higher positive YED. Relative preferences and income levels matter.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Explain why the products might have different YED values.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: Consumers typically continue buying necessities when income changes, which may yield low positive YED; discretionary luxuries may have higher positive YED. Relative preferences and income levels matter.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: Necessities are not necessarily income-inelastic for every market, and some products can be inferior.

skill_specimens.original_case: A fictional premium-trip business estimates YED +1.5 and forecasts a 10% fall in its customers' incomes.
skill_specimens.teaching_note: Using a local approximation, demand might fall by about 15% if other factors and elasticity remain similar. The business could review premium inventory, cash flow and lower-priced alternatives.
skill_specimens.original_practice_prompt: Estimate the directional effect and suggest one cautious response.
skill_specimens.unscored_expected_reasoning: Using a local approximation, demand might fall by about 15% if other factors and elasticity remain similar. The business could review premium inventory, cash flow and lower-priced alternatives.
skill_specimens.misconception_to_challenge: Elasticity is not a precise sales forecast; context, substitution and consumer confidence may alter the outcome.
